item.title: E11 - How Workplace Metaphors Enforce Power
item.description:
Who an organization's "shared" metaphors belong to. It moves from organization studies treating race as absent and organizations as racial structures, to what discrimination metaphors like the glass ceiling reveal and conceal, to a critical realist account of metaphor and political interest, with a "benevolent patriarch" CEO and familistic dependence as the case. It asks whose experience a common metaphor encodes, who can make it stick, and how a researcher would tell a shared metaphor from an imposed one.
Sources: Nkomo (1992); Ray (2019); Bendl & Schmidt (2024); Reed (2024); Prince et al. (2019).

item.title: E10 - How Wrong Metaphors Kill Strategic Initiatives
item.description:
How metaphor and analogy work when a leader frames a change for the people who have to live it. It centers on Cornelissen, Holt & Zundel's (2011) conditions for a frame winning support, especially cultural familiarity and connection to stakeholders' prior motivations, the closest published statement of MAALF's alignment idea, and tests them against Marshak's mismatched change metaphors, conflicting uses of metaphor in change, and sensegiving. It ends on whether a dissonant frame always fails and whether leaders read their audience's metaphors or supply new ones.
Sources: Cornelissen, Holt & Zundel (2011); Marshak (1993); Palmer & Dunford (1996); Cassell & Lee (2012); Gioia & Chittipeddi (1991); Biscaro et al. (2025).

item.title: E9 - Why Abstract Leadership Visions Fail
item.description:
Andrew Carton's work on how leaders' language shapes what work means. It covers how Kennedy and NASA leaders tied everyday tasks to the moon goal, then why image-based visions outperform abstract ones and why leaders default to blurry ones. It ends on questions for my study: whether DREAM's moon language is a metaphor or a concrete image, and whether Carton treats the meanings staff already hold as something leaders read or something they create.
Sources: Carton (2018); Carton, Murphy & Clark (2014); Carton & Lucas (2018).

item.title: E8 - Metaphors as an Organizational X-Ray Machine
item.description:
Sensemaking and sensegiving, the literature a reader is most likely to hold up against "metaphor discernment." It covers how leaders shape others' interpretations of change and the field's open problems, then the education versions: implementers reading policy through what they already believe, teachers making sense of policy together, and McLaughlin on local will and capacity. It closes with a first pass at Carton's work on leader language.
Sources: Gioia & Chittipeddi (1991); Maitlis & Christianson (2014); Spillane, Reiser & Reimer (2002); Coburn (2001); McLaughlin (1987); Carton, Murphy & Clark (2014); Carton & Lucas (2018); Carton (2018).

item.title: E7 - Why Charter Networks Recreate Bureaucracy
item.description:
Optional. Two background questions. First, how institutional logics explain an organization holding competing systems of meaning, and how that compares with a metaphor lens. Second, how school networks and districts divide work between a central office and schools, and what pressures shape charter organizations as they scale.
Sources: Thornton, Ocasio & Lounsbury (2012); Cooney & Cohen (2024); Godart et al. (2024); Peurach et al. (2019); Huerta & Zuckerman (2009); Torres (2022).

item.title: E6 - Eliciting and Analyzing Organizational Metaphors
item.description:
How organizational and educational metaphors have been studied. It sorts the methods by approach: reconstructing metaphors from naturally occurring talk, asking people for a metaphor directly, structured elicitation (Clean Language, ZMET, imaginative elicitation), and using Morgan's images as a lens. It spends time on trustworthiness and on which studies combine inductive and deductive steps, and in what order.
Sources: Schmitt (2005); Cornelissen et al. (2008); Low (2017); Armstrong, Davis & Paulson (2011); Tosey, Lawley & Meese (2014); Oswick & Montgomery (1999); Kirk (2023); Nardon & Hari (2021); Prince & Forr (2021); Rowland et al. (2021); Bruni & Biscaro (2024); Alvesson, Gabriel & Sandberg (2024).

item.title: E5 - Metaphor Alignment in Adaptive School Leadership
item.description:
Debate. Two hosts argue over the gap claim in my own drafts: that no existing work connects a leader's reading of an organization's metaphors to the interventions the leader makes and how staff receive them. One defends the gap. The other argues it's overstated, citing Marshak, Whang, institutional logics, and sensemaking research. They press on whether "discernment" differs from ordinary sensemaking and whether the four quadrants earn their keep, then land on the narrowest version of the gap both will accept.
Sources: Chapter 1 v3 and Chapter 2 framework drafts; Marshak (1993); Whang (2021); Biscaro et al. (2025); Cassell & Lee (2012); Samier (2019); Heifetz et al. (2009); Cooney & Cohen (2024); Gioia & Chittipeddi (1991); Spillane et al. (2002).

item.title: E4 - Why Wrong Metaphors Trigger Staff Resistance
item.description:
The difference between metaphors people hold about leaders and the metaphors a leader has to read in the organization around them. The center is Marshak's four change metaphors and his argument about what happens when a leader's language doesn't fit the change, the closest precedent to MAALF's idea of alignment. It also covers change agents' metaphors in use, leader metaphors like gardener and commander, middle leaders who called themselves "spies," and a CEO cast as a benevolent patriarch, with what that suggests for an organization that calls itself a family.
Sources: Marshak (1993); Cassell & Lee (2012); Alvesson & Spicer (2011); Lumby & English (2010); Samier (2019); Grice (2019); Prince et al. (2019).

item.title: E3 - Why Adaptive Leadership Needs Metaphor Analysis
item.description:
The adaptive leadership side of the study. It covers technical problems versus adaptive challenges, the observe-interpret-intervene cycle, and what interpretation involves in Heifetz's account, including whether shared language or metaphor shows up there at all. It then looks at how adaptive leadership has been studied in schools and takes up Cojocar's question of whether it is a theory or a derivative.
Sources: Heifetz, Grashow & Linsky (2009); Heifetz & Linsky (2017); Cojocar (2009); Pak et al. (2020); Coviello (2025); Sims et al. (2023).

item.title: E2 - Using Metaphors to Lead School Change
item.description:
What Morgan's Images of Organization teaches, what it's for, and where later scholars push past it. It covers reading an organization through several metaphors at once, metaphor and metonymy, conflicting uses of metaphor in change writing, and resonance and dissonance, with Whang's study of Taiwanese middle schools as the school example. Two questions run through it: whether "metaphor" and "image" mean different things, and whether anyone links reading an organization to what a leader does next.
Sources: Morgan (2006, 2011, 2016); Örtenblad, Putnam & Trehan (2016); Schoeneborn, Vásquez & Cornelissen (2016); Palmer & Dunford (1996); Cornelissen et al. (2008); Biscaro et al. (2025); Whang (2021); Oxford Handbook of Metaphor in Organization Studies, chs. 1-3.

item.title: E1 - How Metaphors Dictate Organizational Reality
item.description:
Why a set of metaphors can work as a shared system people think and act through. It covers Lakoff and Johnson's core ideas (mapping, entailment, systematicity, highlighting and hiding, UP/DOWN orientation) and the organization-theory debates that followed. The running question is what would count as evidence that a metaphor is shared across an organization rather than one speaker's turn of phrase.
Sources: Lakoff & Johnson (2003); Gibbs (2008); Tsoukas (1991); Cornelissen (2005); Oswick, Keenoy & Grant (2002); Cornelissen & Kafouros (2008).
